ops.old: A new patient office visit of moderate complexity (CPT 99204) generated a total RVU of approximately 3.0 before the 2021 E&M revision. A single colonoscopy (CPT 45378) generated approximately 3.8 total RVUs for roughly the same physician time investment. The physician doing screening colonoscopies at high volume could generate two to three times the annual revenue of an equally trained physician doing complex diabetes or heart failure management.
ops.new: Before the 2021 E&M revision, a new patient office visit of moderate complexity (CPT 99204) carried 2.43 work RVUs for a typical 45 minutes of physician time, while a diagnostic colonoscopy (CPT 45378) carries about 3.2 work RVUs for a procedure of shorter duration — so a physician performing colonoscopies at high volume generates far more work RVUs per hour than an equally trained physician managing complex diabetes or heart failure.
ops.claim: 99204 total RVU ~3.0 pre-2021; colonoscopy ~3.8 total RVU "for same time"; 2-3x annual revenue
ops.sources: CMS Physician Fee Schedule RVU files (via fastrvu.com/AAPC lookups): 92928 wRVU ~9.75-10.96 depending on year; 45378 wRVU ~3.2; 99204 wRVU 2.43 (2020) -> 2.60 (2021); 99205 3.17 -> 3.50; 99214 1.50 -> 1.92 (CY2021 PFS final rule); 99204 typical time 45 min (pre-2021 CPT descriptor)
ops.note: Total-RVU figures were wrong (99204 total was ~4.6 non-facility in 2020); restated on a work-RVU basis; unverifiable revenue multiple dropped.

ops.new: After a 5.4% cut took effect in 2002, Congress overrode the formula's scheduled cuts — which had grown past 20% in a single year by 2014 — through 17 short-term "doc fix" patches,
ops.claim: SGR cumulative cuts ~30%; Congress overrode "every single year"

ops.old: Research by Khullar and colleagues at Weill Cornell has documented that physicians in high-wRVU environments report significantly higher rates of burnout, with primary care physicians experiencing the highest moral distress when productivity targets conflict with relationship-based care.
ops.new: Productivity pressure and lack of time are among the most commonly cited drivers of physician burnout, and the pressure is sharpest in primary care, where productivity targets collide with relationship-based care.
ops.claim: Khullar et al. (Weill Cornell) documented higher burnout in high-wRVU environments; PCPs highest moral distress
